extracted.intended_audience: Appellants in ex parte appeals before the PTAB (patent practitioners and pro se inventors)
extracted.subtask_short: PTAB ex parte appeal brief drafting
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting and formatting an initial ex parte Appeal Brief to the Patent Trial and Appeal Board, including required statements, organization of arguments, evidence use, and claims appendix rules. Covers what to include, how to prioritize and present arguments, and procedural limits on issues the Board will consider.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brief filing sequence and Reply constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: In most ex parte appeals an initial brief (Appeal Brief), an Examiner’s Answer, and optionally a Reply Brief are filed, in that order. The Reply Brief only needs to include an Argument section and cannot include any new arguments, except to respond to new or different arguments raised in the Examiner’s Answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As the appellant you file the initial Appeal Brief. You are not required to file a Reply Brief, but you may do so to respond to the Examiner’s Answer. The Reply can only respond to arguments in the Answer; it cannot introduce new arguments unless the Examiner raises new or different arguments in the Answer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real party in interest statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a statement identifying the real party in interest at the time the appeal brief is filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A real party in interest may include the inventor and any other individuals or entities with ownership rights. No statement required if named inventor(s) are the real party in interest; absent a statement, Board will consider inventor(s) to be the real party. Typical for pro se inventors. See MPEP §§ 301, 324, 1205.02(i). Example phrasing shown in template.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of related appeals, interferences, and trials
rubrics_metrics.description: List all prior or pending cases before the Board or a court related to the application subject to the current appeal (based on applications or patents you own).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide case numbers and dates of prior decisions where applicable, or state there are none. It is important because related cases could affect or be affected by the Board’s decision. No need to provide copies of decisions. See MPEP § 1205.02(ii).

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary of claimed subject matter (optional for pro se)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a concise explanation of the subject matter defined in each rejected independent claim, including references to supporting portions of the original-filed specification and drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a short explanation of each independent claim with references to (1) supporting aspects of the original-filed specification by page/line or paragraph number and (2) drawings by reference numerals. Pro se applicants may omit this section, but it may help the Board understand issues. See MPEP § 1205.02(iii) and § 1205.02(v).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose which rejections and claims to address (prioritize arguments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide which grounds of rejection and which claim(s) to address in the Appeal Brief; you do not have to address all rejections or pending claims, but arguments not presented will not be considered by the PTAB later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review the case history and law to decide. Consider highlighting strongest arguments first; weaker arguments can distract. Keep in mind that any arguments you do not include cannot be presented later (e.g., in a Reply Brief).

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument organization and headings
rubrics_metrics.description: Argue each ground of rejection under a separate heading identifying the ground (claim number(s), statutory basis, and applied reference(s)). Claims subject to the same ground may be argued individually, as a group, or in subgroups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the same argument applies to multiple claims, argue them as a group under a single heading rather than repeating. If different arguments apply to particular claims, use separate sub-headings for those claims. Use clear headings such as 'Whether claims 1–3 are unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. § 103 over Iranpour in view of Stroud' and then discuss individual claims or subparts as needed. See MPEP § 1205(c)(1)(iv).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain examiner burden and appellant response requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that the examiner initially bears the burden to support a rejection (prima facie case); only after that burden is met does it shift to the appellant to show the rejection is improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner must clearly state reasons for the rejection (e.g., reasons to combine references for an obviousness rejection). For each ground you address, explain in clear terms why the examiner erred. Do not merely assert error without reasons and supporting evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of persuasive errors to identify
rubrics_metrics.description: When arguing a rejection is improper, you may show the examiner (1) misunderstood the invention or claims, (2) misunderstood the cited prior art, and/or (3) misunderstood or misapplied the law or legal basis for the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support assertions with evidence (specification citations, dictionary definitions, case law). Explain specifically why the examiner’s interpretation is inconsistent with the specification or is overly broad/unreasonable. Provide examples and suggested wording to explain misinterpretation of claim terms or prior art teachings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of annotated drawings and record evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider using annotated drawings to explain differences between the claimed invention and cited prior art, and direct attention to evidentiary items in the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotated drawings can make differences clearer for the PTAB. You may rely on affidavits or declarations in the record to support arguments, but such evidence must have been before the examiner during prosecution; otherwise it will not be considered by the PTAB. Examples given where declarations explain why references do or do not suggest combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper hindsight and requirement for explicit reasoning to combine references
rubrics_metrics.description: Argue that an examiner’s suggestion to combine references for obviousness must be supported by explicit reasoning and cannot be based on impermissible hindsight using the applicant’s disclosure as a blueprint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To establish a prima facie case of obviousness, the examiner must explain why a person of ordinary skill would have had an apparent reason to combine the references as proposed. The analysis must be explicit—not merely conclusory—and cannot rely on knowledge of the claimed invention (impermissible 'hindsight'). Provide example argument templates to challenge insufficient reasoning to combine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit Appeal Brief to claim rejections (avoid matters left to examiner discretion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on the PTAB to review matters left to an examiner’s discretion (e.g., objections, restriction requirements, refusals to enter an amendment); those may be reviewed only by petition to the Director.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore, limit your Appeal Brief arguments to claim rejections. If you seek review of an examiner’s refusal to admit an amendment or evidence, do so by petition under the appropriate regulation (e.g., 37 CFR § 1.181).

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenge examiner’s characterization of prior art and case citations
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner has misinterpreted or mischaracterized a prior art reference, explain why the reference does not disclose or suggest the claim element; similarly, if cited case law does not support the examiner’s proposition, point out the error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain specifically why the cited reference fails to disclose or suggest the claimed feature. If you know PTAB or federal court decisions that support your position, explain how those cases apply to your facts and require ruling in your favor. Examples provided for misapplied and supportive cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusion section (optional summary and requested relief)
rubrics_metrics.description: Optionally include a Conclusion summarizing overall positions and the particular decision requested (normally reversal of final rejection and allowance of pending claims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If included, state clearly the decision requested (e.g., reversal and remand for allowance). Provide date and signature block in closing as shown in template.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims appendix content and formatting requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a Claims Appendix containing all claims involved in the appeal, properly formatted and without non-involved claims or non-admitted amendments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims in the appendix should be clean (no brackets or underlining indicating prior amendments), double-spaced, and start on a new page. Do not include canceled or withdrawn claims that are not involved in the appeal. Do not reference any non-admitted amendment. To remove claims from consideration, submit an amendment to cancel them (see 37 CFR §§ 41.31(c), 41.33). See MPEP § 1205.02(v).
